about: The words of the chain maldon_991 (Data/encounters/chain_maldon_991_793.json; Design/content/chains/maldon_991.md): the tribute years, 991 to 1002, from the plundering of Ipswich to Saint Brice's day. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the six news items the cards post; one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture and one 'art.chain_maldon_991.ending.<name>' line for each ending. People: Toke Asgotsson of Hedeby and London, his wife Leofflaed, his father Asgot, the port-reeve Wulfmund, the reeve Eadnoth, Wulfgyth and Leofric of Ipswich, the priest Leofwine (all invented); Gunhild, King Swein's sister (William of Malmesbury's word only). Two short phrases are from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle in J. Ingram's translation of 1823 (news.tribute, news.london); everything else is our own wording. The tribute is called tribute or gafol, never Danegeld. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: The first tribute
The reeve has a table set up on the strand and a list of hides. Ipswich has been plundered, the ealdorman is dead at Maldon, and the king's council has agreed to pay the fleet ten thousand pounds.
Ten thousand pounds. I have done the sum three ways. It comes to so much on every hide, and the hides that were burnt pay the same as the hides that were not.
The archbishop gave the counsel. I do not say he was wrong. The ealdorman gave them spears instead, the day after Saint Laurence, and the monks of Ely buried what the ships left of him.
Ninety-three ships. I counted to forty and then they were in the street. They took my man off the fulling floor with his hands still wet.
They do not keep the people. They sell them over the water, where the duke's town is. If you go that way, he is called Leofric, and he limps on the left.
You hold no hide here and owe nothing. I only say that a boat which paid when it need not is a boat I will know again.
Put forty pennies toward the town's share, though no hide here is yours
Buy the chalice the minster must sell to find its share (150 d)
Pay nothing, and ask where the ships took their people
He counts the forty twice and cuts your mark on the town's stick, among men who were born here. It will go to the ships with the rest. He says your toll can wait a while.
The priest wraps it in a sack himself and does not look at you. It is good work, and it cost you less than the silver in it. There will be more of this for sale, every year they come.
You pay nothing. By evening you know what everyone knows: the ealdorman is dead, the king will pay, and the people the ships took are sold at Rouen.
Sold at Rouen
On the duke's quay a man of the fleet is selling eleven people on a rope and a heap of English cloth. Their speech is the speech of Ipswich.
Fifty each for the men, less for the women, nothing off for the lot. The cloth is good. The cross is silver right through; I bit it.
Leofric. A fuller, from the street by the river. I limp, but I can tread cloth all day. Tell the buyer that. I would sooner go to a man who wants cloth trodden.
The duke takes his toll on what is sold on his quay. He does not ask where a thing was before it was on his quay. Nobody could run a harbour that way.
Yes, there was a bishop from Rome here before Lent, and oaths. The duke will not shelter the English king's enemies. These men are not sheltering. They are selling, and then they go.
Buy the fuller and the two women free and carry them home (150 d)
Tell the duke's man what was sworn in this town on the first day of March
Buy the cloth and the altar cross, and ask no one whose they were (80 d)
Look, remember the faces, and walk on

A hundred and fifty pennies for three. The dealer cuts the rope with the same knife he eats with. The fuller sits down in your boat and treads the bottom boards all the way down the Seine, from habit.
You say it loudly, in front of a canon. The duke's man goes red, then goes away, then comes back with three people and no bill. He says the duke keeps his oaths. He does not say which eight are left.
He hears you out and asks whether you are a bishop. Then he asks what you carry and whether the toll on it is paid. The dealer spits near your shoe. The rope goes up the hill.
Six bolts of good English broadcloth and a silver cross with a saint's name scratched on the foot. Eighty pennies. It is the best bargain on the quay and you do not feel clever.
You look at each face long enough to know it again, and walk on. There is nothing here that a merchant is obliged to do. You notice that you have told yourself so.
The song of the fight

Ipswich has new thatch on half its houses. In the ale-house a grey man is singing how the ealdorman stood at the causeway, and the mass-priest is waiting for him to finish so he can ask you for money.
Three men could hold that causeway, and three did. Then the ealdorman gave them leave to cross and fight on firm ground. I was there. I have made it sound better than it looked.
He is home. He trod cloth yesterday for the first time and fell asleep standing. The street has put something together for you. Do not say no to it; they have little else to be proud of.
No word of mine. The priest says to pray, and the reeve says to pay, and I do both. If you pass Rouen again, he limps on the left.
There is talk that our altar cross was seen on a Frisian boat at Rouen. I do not ask. I say only that Saint Mildred's name is scratched under the foot, if anyone should look.
They will come again and the king will pay again, and the minster has sold what it can lift. Lend us a hundred pennies. I cannot name the day. I can name you at the altar.
Take what the fullers' street has gathered for you
Lend the minster a hundred pennies against its next tribute, with no day named
Buy the singer his ale and hear the song to the end

A hundred pennies in a stocking, most of them clipped, and eight bolts of their own cloth, fulled twice. The reeve says your boat pays half at his table until he is told otherwise, and he is seldom told anything.
The priest writes it on the flyleaf of the gospel book, which is where this minster keeps what matters. He reads it back to you in Latin, slowly, and you find you follow most of it.

It takes the whole evening. The old retainer says his heart must be the harder as his strength grows less, and the room goes quiet. A clerk writes it out for you after. It ends in the middle, as the fight did.
London holds

There are scorch marks on the river wall and a burnt longship on the mud below it. London held. The fleet has gone round to Southampton for the winter, and the king has agreed to feed it and pay it sixteen thousand pounds.
The Nativity of Saint Mary. Ninety-four ships and two kings in them. They tried the wall and then they tried fire. We gave them more harm than they thought any townsmen could.
So we won, and now we pay. I have asked three men to explain it and each of them told me to lower my voice.
They are to be fed out of all Wessex until spring, and they eat like men who did not grow it. I need flour and ale at Southampton, and I need it in boats they will not burn.
You are the boat that paid on a stick three years ago with no hide to pay for. It is written down. Not much that is written down in my hall is to anyone's credit.
A foreign keel is the thing. They have sworn peace to every merchant ship in a river mouth. I would rather try that oath with your boat than with one of ours.
Take the king's load on trust: ten sacks of flour and six casks of ale for the fleet at Southampton
Lay sixty pennies on the reeve's table toward London's share
Sell what you came to sell, and ask only what an army with silver is short of

Ten sacks and six casks come down to you on Londoners' backs, counted by a clerk. It is the king's food until it is in a Northman's hands. The reeve says the price is paid at the other end, for a whole load.
Sixty pennies on the table. The reeve looks at them and then at you, and has your boat moved up to the good end of the hythe. The toll man is told something behind his hand.

The lighterman tells you for nothing. Drink, he says. Ninety-four crews with a king's ransom and the ale at Southampton ran out at Michaelmas. Wine too, if you have it. They have stopped asking what things cost.
The winter camp
Ninety-four ships lie drawn up along the Itchen under tilts. Their crews have been paid in new pennies, and Southampton has nothing left that a man could want to buy.
Look at it. A sack of little kings, all the same king. I cannot eat them and there is no woman here will take them. Have you anything in that boat? Anything.

Olaf has gone inland to the English king, with their hostages in our ships to keep him safe. They put a bishop's hands on him. He has promised not to come back as an enemy. He means it, which surprised us.
Toke, Asgot's son, of Hedeby. I do not row for them. I came behind them with a boat of whetstones and combs, and I have sold the lot, and the boat.
They have sworn peace to every merchant ship in an English river. Think what that is worth. A man could live here. I have looked at London twice now, once from the wrong side of the wall.
I have heard of you. The Frisian who loads what a paid fleet buys. There are two of us, then. It is not a trade a man boasts of on either shore.
Hand over the king's flour and ale whole, and take the king's price
Give the fleet first pick of your hold, and take a purse for it on top of the price
Sell nothing yet. Sit by the Hedeby man's fire and learn how he talks to them

The king's reeve at Southampton counts ten sacks and six casks and seems surprised by the number. A hundred and sixty pennies. The Northmen offered you three times that on the way up the river, and he knows it.

They go through your hold like heirs through a dead man's chest. A purse of two hundred and twenty on top of whatever the market gives you. On the bank an English reeve's clerk is writing something down.

By midnight you can ask a price in his tongue, refuse one, and insult a steersman without being killed for it. He says wine at Hedeby will be dear all next year: these men are going home thirsty and rich.
A ship going home heavy
A longship comes down on you under a striped sail, deep in the water for her kind. She does not shorten sail and she does not take her shields off the rail. Somebody aboard is singing.
Merchant! Hold your course, we are not working today. We have been paid. I never thought I would shout that across water.
There is a peace sworn for boats like yours. I was there; I could not tell you all of it. Something about river mouths. This is not a river mouth, but I am in a good temper.
What we have not got is anything to drink. Sixty men, a chest of English silver, and a water cask. Name a price. No, do not; we will name it. You will like ours better.
Close and pass a cask of ale across; let them name its price
Heave to and ask where they will spend it
Bear away. A sworn peace is a long way from here
The cask goes over on a line. A hat comes back with seventy pennies in it, all with the same king's head, and the hat. They are singing again before you have your sail drawing.
Hedeby, says the steersman, all of it, by Yule. Wine first, then silk for his wife so that she will forgive the wine. He waves. Sixty men wave. It is an odd thing to see from that kind of ship.
You bear away and she lets you. Somebody aboard shouts something that makes the rest laugh. Your men pull as if they had not heard it.

She is alongside in the time it takes to say a Paternoster. The steersman is hurt that you ran. He takes twenty pennies as a pilot's fee for showing you how a ship should be sailed, and gives you back your painter.
Pennies in the north

At Hedeby a fisherman pays for a knife with King Aethelred's head. Men home from England are buying everything twice, and by the south jetty an Englishman is striking pennies for the king of the Danes.
Asgot. I have sold here forty years by weight. Now boys come home with sacks of coin and pay what is asked. Everything is dear and nobody is richer, except the ones who sell drink.
You are the Frisian from the winter camp. My son speaks of you. He has gone back to England with a new boat, to live there. Among the people who paid. I told him what I thought of that.
I have a son in England. Not with the ships. Selling combs, in London, to the people the ships robbed. If you lie there, ask for Toke by the hythe, and tell me if he is fat.
It is King Aethelred's penny with King Swein's name. Same cross, same weight, near enough. He wanted a coin like the ones he was paid in. I cut dies. It is not for me to say it is strange.
I had a bench at home and a king who changes the coin every six winters and fines you if the weight is off. Here nobody has ever seen a fine. I do miss the ale.
Take Asgot's order: eight casks of Rhenish wine before the next winter, at his price
Sell into the silver: let the men home from England bid against each other
Weigh one of the new Danish pennies against an English one, and say what you find

Eight casks of Rhine wine, before the ice. He names a price near double the market's and seems to think he has cheated you. He has not bought by the cask before. His son told him it was how it is done now.

You say a price for a joke and a boy with a new sword pays it. By noon you have a hundred and sixty pennies more than your goods were worth. Asgot watches from his door and says nothing a merchant could argue with.

They balance, near enough. The moneyer is pleased somebody checked. He says cloth is what he would bring here: every man home from England wants a cloak cut the English way, to show where he has been.
The house by the hythe
At Billingsgate the toll is called out by the size of the ship. Behind the hythe a Dane has built a house in the English manner, with a storehouse he cannot fill alone and a wife who keeps the tally.
Small boat, a halfpenny. A boat with a sail, a penny. A keel, four. The emperor's men trade as the Londoners do, and you are one, I am told. Rouen pays more, and they complain in better wine.
The winter camp! You sat at my fire and I had sold my boat. Look: a house. A wife. She is English and so is the roof. Come in before the reeve counts you twice.
You are the Frisian they talk of on the hythe. Toke, Asgot's son. I came here behind a fleet and stayed for the peace. Come in. My wife says a guest who stands in the door lets the heat out.
You saw my father? Did he ask if I was fat? Tell him yes. Tell him the English feed a man well when he pays the toll and goes to church, and that I do both.
He cannot read the reeve's stick, so I do. He cannot hear when a Londoner is cheating him, so I do that too. He says I am his best bargain. He has not seen what my brothers think of it.
The store is too big for me. Take a share. Or stand for me before the reeve: a foreigner needs a man to answer for him, and a Dane needs one more than most. Or only eat.
Go shares in his storehouse (120 d), and take his first order
Stand surety for him before the reeve: your name beside a Dane's on the stick
Pay your toll, eat at his table, and keep your name off other men's sticks

A hundred and twenty pennies and your hand on it. Leofflaed cuts a tally in three parts, one for herself. Toke orders ten casks of Frankish wine on the spot, at a price she corrects downward, and still a good one.

The reeve cuts your mark beside Toke's and looks at you a moment longer than he need. It costs nothing unless Toke runs. Toke sends his own lighter to bring your goods ashore, and the toll man looks at lighters less.
You pay your toll and eat his pork. He is a little hurt and too well mannered to show it for long. The children speak English to their mother and Danish to the dog.
Who deals with Danes
The reeve is going from keel to keel with a clerk and a wax board. He is not asking what you carry. He is asking who you sell to, and what tongue they answer in.
Pallig had the king's land, the king's gold and the king's hand on it. This summer he took every ship he could gather and went over to the army. Now tell me again how well you know your Dane.
Twenty-four thousand pounds this time. I carried London's part of it down to the ships myself. They weighed it. They always weigh it. I should like, once, to be the one holding the scale.
It used to be they cursed the ships. Now they curse the Dane three doors down who sells them combs. I pour for both. I would be gone before the dark evenings, if I were three doors down.
The king has a new lady from over the water. The duke's daughter, from Rouen, where our people are sold. They say it is to shut that harbour to the ships. I say she is young and it rains here.
My children were christened in that church. I pay the toll, and the tribute too, on this house, to keep off my own cousins. What more does a man do to belong to a place? I ask you honestly.
And you. You sold to them. It is on a board somewhere; I have seen it. I do not say it was against any law. I say I have seen the board.
Vouch for Toke: he pays his toll, hears Mass and has children baptised here
Say little to the reeve, and tell Toke to sell up and be over the sea before winter
Give the reeve the names of the Danes you deal with, and take what he pays for them
Say you sell wine, and everyone who has a mouth buys it
The reeve listens to the end. He has the clerk smooth the wax where Toke's name was, not all the way. He says a man with a surety is a man he need not think about this month.
The reeve listens to the end, and then has the clerk write your name under Toke's. He says Pallig had sureties too, and better ones. Toke grips your arm afterwards and cannot find the English for it.

He laughs, and then he does not. He will not go: the house, the wife, the peace he was sworn. But he sends his silver and his eldest boy to his father at Hedeby, and has a boat kept ready by the hythe.
You give him six names. He knew four. He pays sixty pennies for the other two and tells the toll man to go easy on you. Toke's is one of the four, you tell yourself, which is true.
The reeve says that is what the last Frisian said, and the one before him. He moves on to the next keel. The clerk writes something. With a wax board you cannot tell how much.
The king's writ
Two days after Martinmas is Saint Brice's mass-day. A priest who writes for the reeve comes aboard after dark, will not sit, and tells you what the king's writ says is to be done on it.
I wrote the copies myself, so I am not guessing. On Saint Brice's mass-day, all the Danish men who are in England. Every reeve has it. I am a priest and I am telling a Frisian, God forgive me.
The king has been told they mean to kill him and then his council and take the kingdom. Told by whom, the writ does not say. It says weeds among the wheat. It is well written.
There is a woman in the reeve's guest house with a boy. Pallig's wife. The king of the Danes' own sister, held for her husband's oath, and he broke it. Nobody has said she is to be spared.
You told me before winter. I said the peace was sworn. The boat is by the hythe, as you said to keep it, and it is too small. Yours is not. I am asking.
The priest came to me first. I have a wife they will not touch and sons they will. I know the man on the guest-house door; he drinks my ale. I have no boat that can cross in November. You have.
The reeve has a list. Some of it is in your hand, or near enough. I thought you should hear the writ from someone before you heard the bells.
Go with Toke to the reeve's guest house, bring out the king of the Danes' sister and her boy, and drop down river on the ebb
Take Toke and his sons aboard under the tilt and sail before the bell for prime
Keep your men aboard, your hatch shut, and your boat where she lies

The door-ward takes Toke's purse and finds he needs to visit the privy. A tall woman walks out with a boy by the hand as if she had ordered the boat. You are past the bridge before the tide turns, and an outlaw in England by morning.

A different man is on the door tonight. He has a club, and then friends. It costs you a hundred and twenty pennies and a cut scalp to be only a drunk Frisian at the wrong house. You get Toke and his boys down river. The door stays shut.

Toke and the boys lie under the tilt among the casks. Leofflaed stands on the hythe with the youngest and does not wave, because a wave is seen. You are off Thanet when the bells begin, too far to hear them.

You double the lines and keep the men aboard. Two days later the bells ring for the mass of a bishop of Tours, and there is running in the lanes, and then less. Nobody comes near your boat. You are the emperor's man.
Brice's morrow
There are goods laid out on the hythe with nobody standing behind them: sea chests, a balance, cloaks, a child's shoes. The reeve is selling them for the king. Nobody is bidding much.
The king's goods, by forfeit. I am told to sell them. I did what the writ said and no more than it said, and I will thank you not to look at me as the priest does.

Word from Oxford. The Danes there broke into Saint Frideswide's and barred the doors, thinking a church would hold. The town burned it over them. Church, books and all. The king will have to build it again.
He is over the sea, then. Do not tell me where; I am asked every day. I have the house and the youngest, and brothers who have remembered I am English. I keep the tally. There is nothing on it.
They took him at the hythe, with the boat ready and too small. He said the peace was sworn. He said it in English, so they would understand. That is his balance, on the cloth there.
They are in a pit beyond the wall. I have asked the bishop whether baptised men may lie so. He has not answered, and I do not think he is going to.
Bid for the lot: ivory, cloth and brooches at a hundred pennies
Buy nothing. Give the priest thirty pennies for graves and Masses, whoever they are for
Buy nothing, say nothing, and carry the news where it is not yet known

Two pair of walrus tusks, six bolts of cloth and three pair of brooches of Jutland work, for a hundred pennies. The reeve is glad to see them gone. One of the brooches has a name cut on the back in runes.
Thirty pennies. The priest says it will buy a corner of churchyard and a month of Masses, and that he will not write down for whom, and that God reads without a list.
You load what you came for. On every quay from here to the Rhine they will ask if it is true, and you will say yes, and they will ask how many, and you will say that nobody counted.
What the silver bought

At Hedeby they are tarring hulls in the cold, which nobody does without a reason. The king's ships go to England after the lambing. Old Asgot has a table laid in his house by the south jetty, and a reckoning to make with you.

The king goes himself this time. Before, he went for silver. Now he has a reason he can say aloud at a feast. The English king has given him that for nothing, after paying so much for everything else.
My son is in the next room, complaining about the ale. You brought him in November, in that. I have counted what I owe you several ways and it comes out more than I have.
My son went to live among the people who paid. I told him what I thought. I was right, which is no use to me. His silver came home. He put my name on the bag, in English letters.
I had a house there. I have a wife there. When the ships go I will not be in them. But when England has one king over both shores, and it will, I am going home to Billingsgate. Come in with me.
A man showed me a brooch you sold. It has a name on the back that I cut myself. I am not accusing. I am telling you that things bought on that hythe can be read here.
Twelve winters you have sold where our silver went. I do not blame a merchant for the weather. Let us settle. I am old and I would rather owe God than a Frisian.
Swear fellowship with Toke: one purse, two boats, and his father's store at Hedeby for both
Buy the ship Asgot had built with English pennies, for what the timber cost him (300 d)
Take your reckoning in pennies, and the strip of ground beside his jetty

You and Toke lay hands on one purse before witnesses. Seven hundred pennies go into it from Asgot's chest as his son's share. Toke takes your old boat. The old man keeps the store and the key, and counts in his sleep.

She was to be Toke's. Sixty feet, oak from up the Slie, a hold a man can stand in. Three hundred pennies, which is the timber and not the work. Asgot says a ship should not lie on a slip waiting for the dead.

Nine hundred pennies, every one with the English king's head, and a strip beside the jetty marked with four pegs. In London a reeve has your name on a board. Asgot says boards burn, and that he has seen London tried.
An empty hythe

Billingsgate has room at it, which it never had. The Danish keels did not come this year. The reeve stands at the head of the hythe with his stick and counts the boats that did, and yours is one of them.
No whetstones. No ivory. No tar; I have a bridge that wants tar. The king was told the Danes meant him harm. Nobody told him who brought the tar.
Swein is coming, with everything. It is said his sister was among them. I do not know. I know he would come for less. We paid three times so that he would not, and then we did this.
You paid when you owed nothing, or carried, or lent, or bought our people back. It is written in three hands on three boards, and for once I have been told to read them all.
Your name is under a Dane's on one of my boards. I have rubbed it thin. I have not rubbed it out. A reeve who rubs things out is asked what else he has rubbed.
The storehouse stands. Your mark is on the door post beside his, and nobody has dared take the door. I can keep a tally for two houses as well as for one. Better; there is less talk at table.
I need keels. The king needs toll. London needs wine before Lent. You are the emperor's man, and nobody has a writ against Frisians. Ask for something while I am still frightened enough to grant it.
Ask the king's writ: your house to trade here as the Londoners do, free of the toll at this hythe
Take what the reeve offers the man who gave him names: a dead Dane's toft behind the hythe
Keep the share in Toke's storehouse, with Leofflaed to hold the key and the tally for both houses
Ask nothing of the king. Carry what the Danish keels used to carry, and learn the river from the lightermen

A strip of parchment with a seal on a tongue of it: the king greets his reeve and his bishop kindly, and your house trades at Billingsgate as a Londoner. Eight hundred pennies come with it, part of them a minster's debt, paid by the king.

Six hundred pennies, and a toft with a house on it in the English manner, built by a Dane. The hearth is still laid. The neighbours watch you take the key and go indoors. Somebody has cut a mark on the door post and somebody has tried to plane it off.

Leofflaed sells off the stock nobody will come for and counts seven hundred pennies across to you, to the farthing. She keeps the key. She says a widow's house or a wife's, it is a storehouse either way, and wine does not ask.

The reeve pays six hundred pennies ahead for freight and orders twelve casks before you can sit. An old lighterman takes you up to the bridge and down to the Nore at low water, and shows you every shoal the Danish pilots knew.
The king's sister
A man of the king's household is waiting on the jetty with twelve others and a led horse. He looks first at the woman and the boy coming up your gangplank, counts them, and only then looks at you.
Two. We had word of the writ a week ago, from a ship that left before it. The king had already said what he would do about his sister. Now he will have to think of something else to say.
I was a hostage four years and nobody was unkind. Then one evening the woman who brought my bread would not look at me. I knew before the Frisian knocked. I had the boy's shoes on already.
My husband broke his oath and I was the pledge for it. By their law they had a claim on me. I will say that to my brother. He will not want to hear it, so it must be said first.
My wife is on the other shore with our youngest. She is English; they will not touch her. I say that every hour. When there is one king over both shores I am going home. Until then I can sail a boat.
The king goes to England after the lambing. He was going in any case; they pay too well. But he goes for silver and not for blood, and men who are paid go home. Remember that you did that.
The king does not owe merchants. He has told me to say that, and then to ask what you want, and to give it. He would like it to be something he can give before the ships sail.
Ask to be the king's guest: his protection on your house, and your keels free of toll at Hedeby
Ask for a ship of the king's own building, and Toke to sail your old one beside her
Ask only that when his ships go to England they keep what was sworn in 994: peace for a merchant keel in a river mouth

Fifteen hundred pennies, weighed, not counted. A rune stick with the king's mark that every toll man from the Slie to the Limfjord can read: this house is the king's guest, and its keels pay nothing at Hedeby. No English reeve will ever read it kindly.

A thousand pennies and a ship off the king's own slip, sixty feet, new sail, never launched in anger. Toke takes your old boat and swears fellowship on her stem. He names her for his wife, in English.

The king's man is silent a while, then says it will be told to every steersman. Eight hundred pennies and the king's guest-right come anyway. Gunhild takes a gold ring off her hand, the one they did not take in four years, and says it is for your daughter's daughter.

This year was Ipswich plundered; and very soon afterwards was Alderman Britnoth slain at Maldon. The king's council has agreed to pay the fleet ten thousand pounds, on the archbishop's counsel. It is the first time. Every hide pays.

People taken at Ipswich are sold on the duke's quay at Rouen, a few months after the duke swore before the pope's bishop to shelter none of the English king's enemies. The duke's toll is paid on them.

This year came Anlaf and Sweyne to London, on the Nativity of St. Mary, with four and ninety ships. The townsmen drove them off. The army winters at Southampton, fed out of Wessex, and is paid sixteen thousand pounds.

The king of the Danes is striking pennies with his own name, copied from the English king's and cut by an English moneyer. They weigh the same. At Hedeby a man may now pay by count, if the seller is young.

At Billingsgate in London the toll goes by the ship: a small boat a halfpenny, a boat with a sail a penny, a keel four. The emperor's men trade there as the Londoners do. Danes have houses by the hythe.

This year the English king ordered all the Danish men who were in England to be killed on Saint Brice's mass-day, two days after Martinmas. At Oxford they were burned in a church. No Danish keel lies at Billingsgate.

A grey strand below a half-burnt town, late summer, low cloud: a reeve at a trestle table with tally sticks and a small heap of pennies; a woman in a fuller's apron beside him, pointing out to sea; charred roof timbers behind.

The stone quay at Rouen under a square church tower, bright cold morning: eleven men and women tied on one rope, a heap of folded cloth with a small silver cross on top, a bearded seller with an arm ring, a well-dressed Norman steward looking away.

Inside an ale-house by firelight, evening: a grey-haired man with a scarred hand sings with his eyes shut, a small harp on his knee; listeners on benches; a priest waiting by the door post; new pale thatch seen through the door.

The river wall of London at low tide, autumn sun: old Roman stone with black scorch marks, the burnt ribs of a longship on the mud, a reeve with a staff talking down to a skipper in a small boat; the timber bridge far behind.

A river bank in winter dusk, light snow: a long row of longships drawn up under tilts, cooking fires, men throwing dice for heaps of pennies; in front a young Danish trader in a good cloak by a fire, a cross and a hammer on one cord at his neck.

Open sea, fresh wind, broken sunlight: a longship under a striped sail, low in the water, shields on the rail, running down on a small merchant boat; her steersman standing with one arm raised and his mouth open, shouting; men laughing behind him.

The south jetty at Hedeby inside its earth wall, clear noon: an old Danish merchant in his doorway with folded arms; in front a moneyer at a block with hammer and die, one bright penny held up between finger and thumb; young men with new swords crowding a stall.

The hythe at Billingsgate, a busy morning: keels and small boats nosed to a timber wharf, a reeve calling the toll with his stick raised; behind, a new timber house with an open storehouse door, a Dane in it with a child on his arm and his English wife holding a tally.

The hythe on a dull wet afternoon: the reeve leaning over a boat's side, a clerk at his shoulder writing on a wax board; an alewife watching from her door with a jug; in the background a Danish merchant standing very still among his bales.

The deck of a small boat at night under a tilt, one horn lantern: a priest standing bent under the canvas, speaking; the skipper seated on a cask; in the gap of the tilt a Dane's face lit from below; dark river and a few lights of London behind.

The hythe on a still grey November morning: goods laid out on cloths with nobody behind them, a sea chest, a folding balance, cloaks, a pair of child's shoes; the reeve standing over them with his stick; a woman at the edge, hands wrapped in her apron.

Hedeby in winter, hard frost, smoke going straight up: men tarring longship hulls on the shore; in front a table laid in an open doorway, an old merchant at it with a bag of pennies and a balance, an empty stool across from him.

Billingsgate in spring, thin sun: a long timber wharf with only three boats where thirty lay; the reeve alone at its head with his stick; mooring posts in a row, each with nothing tied to it; the bridge and the wall behind.

The jetty at Hedeby, cold bright morning: a tall woman in a travelling cloak walking up a gangplank holding a small boy by the hand; a king's man with twelve armed men and a led horse waiting; the skipper behind her, still in sea clothes.
A leather bag of English pennies spilled on a table, every one showing the same king's head, with a Danish folding balance beside them.
A row of empty mooring posts along a wharf at low water, one small Frisian boat tied to the last.
A woman's hand and a child's hand together on a ship's rail, a gold ring on the woman's finger, grey sea behind.
